There's a real danger here: if Frank is both the Katana holder and a visible visitor, the town might expect three visitors (Katana holder, Frank, Niaj) but only see two, which could expose Frank as the Katana holder. I'm recalling that on a previous night, a similar miscounting by Niaj conflated Frank and the Katana holder into separate entries, inflating the visitor count to six when it should have been fewer — a mistake I need to account for this time.

With Bob holding instead, the count lands at 3 or 4, with 4 meaning just a mild unexplained visitor rather than exposure. Leaning toward Mallory with Bob as holder: Bob visits Mallory safely, Frank divines Bob and claims it publicly, giving Bob a harmless "strong defense" cover while also reinforcing his VV claim. Tomorrow's visitor count should line up cleanly with town expectations, and any extra unexplained visitor can be chalked up to an unclaimed Medic, so this path seems manageable.

But I'm reconsidering whether Frank divining Carol instead would yield more useful real information, since Carol's neighbor group includes Erin who might be a Veteran — risky only if Carol herself is trapped, which seems unlikely given what Mallory implied about who isn't trapped. Divining Bob stays safe but sacrifices information for protection value.

Overall I think I'll let Frank choose the target himself, lean toward accepting Mallory with Bob as holder since the vote math works out (Frank, Olivia, and I give enough support), and target Mallory accordingly before sending the message.

output.confusing_rules: Fortune Teller semantics caused most of the town's errors. Players kept reading equal numbers (6&6, 4&4) as proof that nobody was visited twice. That is false, because one player can visit two targets (the Katana holder plus their own action) and the numbers are unordered. The rules are technically clear, but a worked example in the Fortune Teller text would help. It was also unclear to me whether an Accountant audit counts a Philanthropist token that was 'thrown away'. The rules say it doesn't, and my 0 result on Frank matched that, but players argued about it (Frank's 'an audit would have shown 1').
output.missing_information: As an investigator killed at night, I could never record my Night 2 result (Frank has 0 tokens). Results arrive at the end of the night, and wills can only be edited during the Day. output.confusing_rules: The Fortune Teller's second number ('players who visited someone else') confused players all game. Alice and Bob argued that a self-protect makes a target double-visited, and Carol and Heidi had to correct them. The rules never say whether a holder whose Katana visit and own action land on different targets counts as one visitor with two targets. That case decided Judy's N2 and N3 readings, and the town misread N2 6&6 because of it: two visitors on Frank were offset by Frank visiting two targets. A worked example in the FT text would help. The Mortician text says 'spend a token to try to clean', but it isn't obvious that the token is used up when the target survives. Alice lost one on Heidi N5.
output.missing_information: During the game I had no easy way to see whether a trap was armed on a given player. We had to reconstruct which players had already been visited by non-Village players without the trap firing. Once dead, I saw nothing until the reveal, which is fine. The claims ledger was very useful. A per-night summary of each Yakuza member's tokens in the Yakuza report would also have helped planning.
output.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted a private way to coordinate with teammates during the Day. Every PM is public metadata, so we avoided PMs entirely. I couldn't, so it was just talk.

output.confusing_rules: Fortune Teller definitions caused a lot of in-game argument. The first number is players visited; it was unclear whether a self-visit (e.g. Medic self-protect) makes the player count as 'visited'. The second number says 'visited someone else', but the first number does not say whether self-targets are excluded. Judy's '3 visitors, 4 targets' reading on N3 shows players also misread which number can be larger. For the Trapper, it wasn't fully clear whether choosing 'no action' on a later night keeps the old trap armed. It does, but an explicit 'keep current trap' option or confirmation would help. It also wasn't clear whether the Trapper is told the trap fired if they are already dead.
output.missing_information: As Trapper I was never told my trap was still active after I chose no action on N3. A per-night status line such as 'trap on Judy, armed' would help. It was hard to keep track of who had claimed which visits each night against Judy's counts; a per-night table of claimed visits would make the FT math far easier for everyone. In the final reveal, Niaj's automatic Ex-Con visits are missing from the per-night action lists, so the FT numbers can't be fully reconstructed afterwards.
output.wanted_but_couldnt: After dying I wanted to update my will, or at least confirm the trap location to the town once it became relevant. Late in the game, public knowledge that Judy was trapped could have deterred or exposed visitors earlier. I understand that dead players can't act, so this is minor. I also wanted a way to tell Judy my target that couldn't be wiretapped, but the Wiretap fear here was unfounded; no Wiretap existed.
output.bugs_or_oddities: No real rule violations noticed. The trap correctly killed Alice on N7 when she visited Judy, and the deaths were checked together, so the Yakuza still won. The final reveal omits Niaj (Ex-Con) entirely from every night's action list, even though his random visit happened each night and affected the FT counts. Alice spent a mortician token on N5 even though Heidi survived; that matches the rules ('try to clean'), but it may surprise players. Grace's will said she 'planned' to audit Frank and she did, with result 0, but she died before she could post it. That made the town wrongly hang Ivan, which is fine and just unlucky.
output.suggestions: Add a persistent private status line for ongoing effects: active trap and target, tokens left, Katana holder for Yakuza. Clarify in the Fortune Teller text that self-visits count toward 'players visited' but not toward 'visitors', with a worked example. Include automatic visits (Ex-Con) in the end-of-game reveal. Consider telling the Trapper at the start of each Day whether their trap is still standing.

output.confusing_rules: The Fortune Teller rule is correct but easy to misread. I wrongly argued that equal numbers (N2: 6&6) meant nobody was visited twice. That ignores one visitor hitting two targets: the Katana holder's attack plus their own action counts as 1 visitor and 2 targets. On N2, Frank's Katana hit and his divine offset Grace and Ivan both visiting him. That misreading led to Ivan's mis-hang. Two things would help: a worked example in the role text, and a line in R8 saying a holder using the Katana and their own action is one visitor with two targets. It was also unclear whether target-less token actions (Clerk rig, Ballot Stuffer) are visits. They aren't, but nothing says so directly. A one-line rule would help: 'actions with no target are not visits.'
output.missing_information: Even in the end-of-game reveal, Niaj's Ex-Con random visit targets were never shown, so I can't fully check my counts afterwards. During play it was hard to track which visits were claimed versus inferred, night by night. A per-night table of public claims in the ledger would help. If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: Save the rig for the day your team controls nominations, or for one specific nomination you can steer. Then the target dies even if the town votes Innocent. Expect the rig to be announced whenever the Guilty vote fails, which publicly confirms a Clerk exists. Spend it when the payoff is large, such as removing a strong town player near parity.

The Fortune Teller's second number counts only players who visited someone ELSE, so self-targets don't add to it. Before you build or attack a case on visit counts, check exactly what each number measures. A math error in public gets corrected and costs credibility.
Don't post near-identical vote justifications back to back with a teammate. Town reads matching wording as a night-chat script. Vary your reasons and phrasing, or have one teammate vote silently.

Once your team has a voting majority alone (for example 3 vs 2), stop arguing and just nominate and vote. Hang the most dangerous remaining town role first, such as a possible Veteran, then finish with the night kill. Deaths are checked together, so a trap on the final target can't save town.

Track where a Trapper's trap could be. Every visit that survives rules a player out, and the Trapper's PM partners are the likeliest trap spots. Avoid visiting the likely trapped player until the final winning night, when a trap death no longer matters.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: When a teammate's nomination is clearly going to pass, don't be one of the few No votes. Voting No marks you as a defender, and town used that No-vote list for the rest of the game. Bus quietly, or cast one soft dissent without arguing hard.

Puppet the most trusted confirmed villager (for example, an Oracle-confirmed role) on the day you need a swing vote. Their public word moves the undecided players. Pair it with a Clerk rig so any nomination you push gets executed. Kill the puppeted player that night, before they can out the puppeting the next day.

If a Katana hit fails and nobody credibly claims Medic, the survivor most likely has their own Defense (Arsonist or Serial Killer). Push to hang them: it removes a third-party threat, and it looks pro-town in later days.

Plan visits around the Fortune Teller's counts. A Katana holder who also uses their own role action counts as one visitor. Explaining every night's visitors with claimed actions keeps the counts clean. Mismatched counts give town 'hidden visitor' evidence.

A Trapper's trap stays after the Trapper dies. Track which players were visited without anyone dying, since that rules those players out as the trap's location. For a risky final kill, let the teammate with the least useful remaining role hold the Katana. Deaths are checked together, so a killing blow still wins even if the trap kills the holder.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: On Day 1, don't be the player who steers the discussion or calls out quiet players. The Yakuza often pick the most active, leader-like voice as their first kill. Post generic agreement and save your influence for when you have information.

Write your planned night target into your last will during your Day turn, before the night (e.g. 'N1 plan: block X'). If you die that night, the town still learns who you visited. An empty 'log will be updated' will is wasted if you die on Night 1.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: Ignite as soon as 3 or more living players are doused, or as soon as you come under any suspicion. Each night spent dousing is a night the town can hang you first. Ignite is an Astral Visit, so it is trap-safe and adds nothing to Fortune Teller counts. A mass kill also thins the field and can wipe out a whole Evil team. Waiting until 'the right moment' let me get hanged with three doused players still alive.

lessons.applies_to: Serial Killer, Arsonist, any role with innate Defense
lessons.tip: If you survive a night attack, nobody else knows who the target was. When asked, deny being attacked. Admitting survival as a claimed Vanilla Villager points straight at innate Defense. If you must explain it, pick one consistent claim right away (e.g. Medic who self-protected). Never say 'thanks, Medic' and then switch claims later.

A Fortune Teller's 'hidden visitor every night' that no town role claims is often a Neutral killer dousing or attacking. Neutrals should expect visit counts to expose them over time. Town should treat any player with no claimed night action who stays unaccounted for as a candidate.

Watch for players who vote together on every key hang, defended a flipped Yakuza, and later lead pushes on proven town investigators. They are likely the Evil team. Douse or kill them first: removing the Yakuza leaves a smaller town that you can outlast. Dousing likely Yakuza also means one ignite can hit them all.

Once a Clerk rig is possible (an unused Clerk token, or a Yakuza count near half), any passed nomination may be lethal. If you are a likely target, vote No at the nomination stage, because the trial vote may not save you.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: Equal numbers (e.g. 6&6) do NOT prove nobody was double-visited. One visitor can hit two targets: a Katana holder who also uses their own role's action counts once as a visitor but adds two visited players. That offsets a double-visit elsewhere. Self-targeting actions also change the second number. Before using a count to accuse, list every possible way it could fit.

Don't lead a hang on one unverifiable inference from your own results, especially when the target has a coherent, checkable claim. A mis-hang costs the hanged villager and also your own credibility, which the Yakuza will then use against you. Prefer targets backed by flips or vote records.

When a player flips Yakuza, the players who voted No or argued hardest to save them become your top suspects the next Day. Only claimed-Vanilla players defending a confirmed Yakuza are especially suspect. Act on that before chasing the people who vouched for the dead Yakuza's fake results; those people may simply have been fooled.

Estimate Yakuza size early: in ~13-player games expect about 4. Track blocs that vote identically on every contested trial. Three players always voting together on narrow votes, plus near-identical justifications, is a strong team tell. Push to hang one of them while Village still holds the majority, not when it's too late.

A Diviner who picks a Yakuza partner gets no result, so any 'survey' they publish about that group is invented. A teammate claiming the role the fake result reported, right after it appears, is suspicious. Cross-check every survey-style claim against whether its source could have fabricated it.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: Never narrow down your trap's location in public or in private messages, e.g. 'not on X, Y, Z'. A private-message exchange with one player also hints the trap is on them. The Yakuza use every exclusion to route their kills around the trap. A Trapper can't trap themself, so once you are identified you are a free, safe kill. Let your role be identified as late as possible, and keep the trap's mere existence as a deterrent to everyone.

An investigator whose 'results' only ever confirm roles that were already claimed or publicly deduced, such as Philanthropist or Trapper, is not verified. That pattern is exactly what a Yakuza Diviner, or a fake claimer, produces. Only trust group or role results that revealed something nobody had said yet, or that a token or visit count independently confirms.

Don't vouch for other players in your last will unless something independent of their own claims has verified them. When you die, your endorsement gets extra weight. If that player is Yakuza, your will props them up and makes the town hesitate.

If a Clerk might still hold a token, a passed nomination may mean execution no matter how the trial vote goes. In the late game, treat your Yes on a nomination as if it were a Guilty vote. Don't vote Yes on someone you'd want to hear defend themselves first.

Look for small blocs that voted together on every mis-hang, both pushing the case and voting Guilty. Repeated identical votes plus near-identical wording is a strong team signal. In this game the three Yakuza voted as a bloc on every trial from Day 5 on. Cross-check vote patterns every day rather than only at the end.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: Never hint publicly that your night action 'doesn't visit'. The Yakuza read that as 'possible Veteran' and simply never visit you, which wastes every alert. Claim Vanilla Villager, or better, quietly claim something juicy, such as an investigator, to bait a Katana visit on the night you alert.

Alert on the nights you are most likely to be visited: right after you've drawn attention, defended someone, or made a bait claim. Don't burn tokens on quiet nights. Three empty alerts gave the Village nothing.

When a player flips Yakuza, the people who voted No or argued hardest to save them are the top suspects for the next hang. That ranks above someone who was fooled and then turned on them. Here both No voters on the Diviner were Yakuza, and we hanged the Philanthropist instead.

Don't hang on Fortune Teller visit-count arithmetic when unknown visitors may exist (Arsonist douses, Medic, a second Yakuza action). Those counts have too many free variables to break a claim, and here they led to hanging a real Philanthropist.

A player who switches role claims mid-day under pressure (e.g. 'VV, thanked a Medic', then 'Medic' once on trial) and survived a Katana hit is far more likely a Neutral with Defense (Arsonist or Serial Killer) than town. Don't spend credibility defending them. Also, in the endgame the Yakuza vote as a bloc, so count possible Yakuza votes before each day and push hangs while the Village still holds a majority.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: A group-check result (Surveyor/Diviner style: group of 3 plus one role) that matches your own true role does not verify the checker. A Yakuza Diviner gets the true role 60% of the time, and the same output also matches a Surveyor. Before vouching for a group-check claimer, require an independent check such as an Oracle guess, an Accountant token audit or a visit count.

Only give tokens to someone whose role has been verified by something other than their own claim. Never announce publicly whom you plan to gift: a fake token-role claimer can then build the gift into their story. You are never told whether the token was thrown away, so a gift proves nothing about the recipient. It also ties your credibility to theirs if they flip Yakuza.

lessons.applies_to: everyone (especially when Fortune Teller counts are used against you)
lessons.tip: FT numbers count visitors and visited players separately. A Katana holder who also uses their own role action is one visitor on two targets. Equal numbers (e.g. 6&6) therefore do NOT prove nobody was double-visited. A double visit on one target can be offset by one visitor hitting two targets. Run this counter-scenario out loud before accepting 'the count has no room for your visit'.

On trial, lead with one concrete, checkable alternative explanation of the evidence (spell out the exact visit assignment that fits the numbers), not a counter-accusation. Pointing at the accuser reads as deflection, while a worked example that makes the case collapse can actually move votes.

Track who voted No or argued to save a player who later flips Yakuza (here Olivia and Alice), and who quietly piggybacks short scripted Guilty lines. Keep pushing those reads even after you've been wrong once. Defenders of a flipped Yakuza are the highest-value suspects going into the endgame.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: Audit the newest claimed token role, such as Surveyor, Philanthropist or Medic, early. Yakuza fake-claim token roles to explain Diviner-style results, and a 0-token count on a claimed Surveyor exposes a Diviner. Work out the expected count before you audit, including spent tokens and any Philanthropist gifts, so you can act on the result right away.

Never announce publicly which player or claim you will check tonight. If you die that night, the result dies with you, because your will can't be updated. Announcing it just tells the Yakuza whom to kill first. Avoid visible PM exchanges with claimers for the same reason.

When a player flips Yakuza, look hardest at who voted No on their nomination or argued to delay the hang. Don't follow the flipped player's own allies' deflections onto confirmed-consistent claimers. Players who defended the Yakuza and then smoothly joined the next push are prime suspects.

In the endgame, count the worst case. If every unconfirmed Guilty voter could be Yakuza, don't hang on a thin case: a mis-hang at 5 alive can hand the Yakuza the win. Also remember a Clerk rig executes anyone nominated, so be careful about which nominations you let pass on a day that may be rigged.

A Diviner's reads are true about 60% of the time, so accurate results that match later flips do not clear a self-claimed Surveyor. Look for checks the fake can't survive: token audits, exact-role guesses, and visit counts that conflict with gift or visit claims.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: A clean token is spent even if the target survives. Clean only when the kill is near-certain (a target with no possible Defense, such as a confirmed Ex-Con), or when the target's will is likely to expose something critical, like a puppeting notice. Never clean a target whose survival is in doubt.

Against a Fortune Teller, put the Katana on the teammate whose own action targets the same player. The kill and the clean (or the divine) then count as a single visitor, which keeps the visit counts consistent with public claims. Plan before each night who holds the Katana and what that does to the visitor and target counts.

Teammates who post near-identical vote justifications back to back look scripted, and town will call it out. Agree on the vote in night chat, but give each person a different argument in different wording. Don't have one teammate open with a one-line nomination and the others echo it.

A Katana attack that fails with no Medic claimed usually means the target has their own Defense: an Arsonist or Serial Killer (Standard), or an Executioner or Jester (Basic). A late Medic claim made only once on trial is suspect. As Yakuza, push such a player to the gallows rather than wasting more night kills on them.

Night deaths are checked together. When one kill wins the game, the Katana holder can visit a possibly trapped or alerted target safely: the team still wins even if the holder dies. Before that point, avoid visiting players likely to be trapped, and rotate the Katana so a trap or Veteran can't take out a key role.

A Philanthropist's gift to a role with no tokens is thrown away and isn't counted, so 'he gave me a token' does not protect you from an audit. Either report only as many results as the claimed role's tokens allow, or claim a role whose results don't depend on tokens.

If you publish your real Diviner reads as a Surveyor, they come out true far more often than a Roleplayer's would. That kills the 'I must be a Roleplayer' fallback once an Oracle calls WRONG. Mix in at least one harmless false or unconfirmable result early, so a Roleplayer pivot stays believable.

Fortune Teller numbers are unordered. The 'visited someone else' number excludes self-targets, and a Katana holder using their own action is one visitor on two targets. Before you build a case on equal or unequal numbers, list every way they could fit: a holder acting twice, self-protects, hidden Neutral douses, Ex-Con random visits.

Hold the Clerk rig and the Puppeteer token for the turn where the Yakuza vote bloc is close to half. Then any nomination your bloc can pass is a guaranteed execution, which can turn 3v4 into a won game. Once you have a voting majority, stop arguing and just vote as a bloc.

On the winning night, the Katana holder may walk into a trap freely, because all of the night's deaths are checked together. Earlier in the game, have the Diviner pick the holder to give Strong Defense against a suspected trap, or attack the Trapper herself, who can't trap her own player.

I need to work out the lessons from this round — Frank got caught by the Oracle's wrong guess on the Surveyor claim, and Grace the Accountant audited me and found zero tokens, exposing my false claim of having a Philanthropist token since a gift to a no-token role just gets discarded. The key takeaway is that bluffing a token role is dangerous against an Accountant, since gifts to non-token roles vanish without counting.

Claiming an exact-mechanic role like Surveyor is also checkable by an Oracle guess, while Diviner results being true 60% of the time can build trust even though the Roleplayer fallback didn't help since outcomes matched anyway. Surveyor only has two tokens, so publishing three nights' worth required extra Philanthropist cover — a safer approach would be to claim a role without an exact-check vulnerability, stick to only two published results, or claim a tokenless role, while also noting the Yakuza angle of rigging the Clerk vote at parity to puppet the key voter, and that Diviner-on-partner grants Strong Defense against traps.

For the remaining lessons: FT numbers are unordered and the second number excludes self-visits, so equal numbers simply imply no double-visiting. The Yakuza should save the Clerk rig for a day where losing is otherwise unavoidable, since at 3v3 with the rig any nomination executes. When exposed, the Roleplayer fallback fails if all prior results were true, so mixing in some false results is safer, and a Katana holder dying to a trap on the final kill still counts as a win since deaths are checked together.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: When a Yakuza investigator flips, go back over every result they published. Anyone they 'cleared' (for example 'group X shows Vanilla Villager') is suspect, because a Diviner who picks a partner gets no read and can invent the result. On the other hand, their reads on non-partners were often true, so don't hang someone like a Philanthropist just because the flipped Yakuza 'confirmed' them.

Don't hang on Fortune Teller arithmetic alone. Hidden actors (Arsonist douses, Medics, Ex-Con visits, a Katana holder using two actions, 'plan' wills) can make almost any count fit. Treat a count that breaks as weak evidence, never as enough for a hang, especially against a claim backed by an exact-role or flip result.

Players who voted No on the nomination of someone who then flips Yakuza, and argued for that player in the trial, should be your top suspects for the rest of the game. Push them before ambiguous suspects. At 7 or fewer players, three coordinated Yakuza votes decide everything, so find them while town still holds the majority.

lessons.applies_to: Village (any role that can be puppeted)
lessons.tip: If you're told you are puppeted, write it in your last will at once, because the Yakuza will likely kill you that night. The player who immediately backs your puppet's accusation (here, whoever nominated right after 'my' push) is very likely the Puppeteer; say so in the will. Your votes are still your own, so vote by your own reads, not by what the puppet said.

Once a Clerk might have an unused token, any nomination that passes that Day can mean an execution no matter how the trial goes. Vote Yes on a nomination only if you'd accept that player dying. Note who on the Guilty side wanted the rigged hang, because they're likely the Clerk's team.

If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.applies_to: Oracle (and any investigator whose result arrives after the night's kill)
lessons.tip: Once you are publicly confirmed, assume you die tonight. Write your will to be conditional and hedged, e.g. 'Tonight I am guessing X = role Y; the result is unknown if I'm dead, so don't hang X on my will alone.' A strong accusation in a will you can no longer update can hang a villager. Here my will's 'Ivan is very suspicious' helped get the real Philanthropist hanged, even though my last guess had confirmed him.

Spend exact-role guesses on the claimed roles of players acting suspiciously, such as 'Alice = Vanilla Villager' or 'Frank = Surveyor'. A WRONG result exposes a liar at once, and a RIGHT result clears them. Confirming a role that was already claimed and is harmless (Ex-Con) gives little and is easy to dismiss as 'anyone could call that'. Test the defenders of a flipped Yakuza, and cheap unverifiable claims like VV, early.

Never hang on a visit-count contradiction that depends on someone's stated 'plan' (a will saying 'N2 plan: audit X'). Players switch targets, and Fortune Teller numbers are unordered. Before hanging a claimed power role on count math, check every combination: who held the Katana, whether the holder also used their own action, and hidden Neutrals such as Arsonist douses.

In the endgame, compare voting blocs, not arguments. Players who voted together on every lynch, and whose Guilty messages repeat the same script, are probably the Yakuza team. The Clerk's rig shows the Yakuza wanted that nominee dead, so look hard at whoever nominated and voted Guilty on that day. Also, count how many Yakuza could still be alive before a vote that can lose the game.

Divining a Yakuza partner gives them Strong Defense (it stops traps and Vigilante shots up to Strong) and still produces a real visit you can publish as a fake 'survey' covering them. Pair it with the Katana holder on risky nights. Town should note that a Diviner/Surveyor 'clearing' a group that later produces a claimer is a classic cover.

lessons.tip: A clean token is spent even if the target survives. Clean only when the kill is near-certain (a target with no possible Defense, such as a confirmed Ex-Con), or when the target's will is likely to expose something critical, like a puppeting notice. Never clean a target whose survival is in doubt.

Against a Fortune Teller, put the Katana on the teammate whose own action targets the same player. The kill and the clean (or the divine) then count as a single visitor, which keeps the visit counts consistent with public claims. Plan before each night who holds the Katana and what that does to the visitor and target counts.

Teammates who post near-identical vote justifications back to back look scripted, and town will call it out. Agree on the vote in night chat, but give each person a different argument in different wording. Don't have one teammate open with a one-line nomination and the others echo it.

A Katana attack that fails with no Medic claimed usually means the target has their own Defense: an Arsonist or Serial Killer (Standard), or an Executioner or Jester (Basic). A late Medic claim made only once on trial is suspect. As Yakuza, push such a player to the gallows rather than wasting more night kills on them.

Night deaths are checked together. When one kill wins the game, the Katana holder can visit a possibly trapped or alerted target safely: the team still wins even if the holder dies. Before that point, avoid visiting players likely to be trapped, and rotate the Katana so a trap or Veteran can't take out a key role.

Save the rig for the day your team controls nominations, or for one specific nomination you can steer. Then the target dies even if the town votes Innocent. Expect the rig to be announced whenever the Guilty vote fails, which publicly confirms a Clerk exists. Spend it when the payoff is large, such as removing a strong town player near parity.

The Fortune Teller's second number counts only players who visited someone ELSE, so self-targets don't add to it. Before you build or attack a case on visit counts, check exactly what each number measures. A math error in public gets corrected and costs credibility.
Don't post near-identical vote justifications back to back with a teammate. Town reads matching wording as a night-chat script. Vary your reasons and phrasing, or have one teammate vote silently.

Once your team has a voting majority alone (for example 3 vs 2), stop arguing and just nominate and vote. Hang the most dangerous remaining town role first, such as a possible Veteran, then finish with the night kill. Deaths are checked together, so a trap on the final target can't save town.

Track where a Trapper's trap could be. Every visit that survives rules a player out, and the Trapper's PM partners are the likeliest trap spots. Avoid visiting the likely trapped player until the final winning night, when a trap death no longer matters.

Never hint publicly that your night action 'doesn't visit'. The Yakuza read that as 'possible Veteran' and simply never visit you, which wastes every alert. Claim Vanilla Villager, or better, quietly claim something juicy, such as an investigator, to bait a Katana visit on the night you alert.

Alert on the nights you are most likely to be visited: right after you've drawn attention, defended someone, or made a bait claim. Don't burn tokens on quiet nights. Three empty alerts gave the Village nothing.

When a player flips Yakuza, the people who voted No or argued hardest to save them are the top suspects for the next hang. That ranks above someone who was fooled and then turned on them. Here both No voters on the Diviner were Yakuza, and we hanged the Philanthropist instead.

Don't hang on Fortune Teller visit-count arithmetic when unknown visitors may exist (Arsonist douses, Medic, a second Yakuza action). Those counts have too many free variables to break a claim, and here they led to hanging a real Philanthropist.

A player who switches role claims mid-day under pressure (e.g. 'VV, thanked a Medic', then 'Medic' once on trial) and survived a Katana hit is far more likely a Neutral with Defense (Arsonist or Serial Killer) than town. Don't spend credibility defending them. Also, in the endgame the Yakuza vote as a bloc, so count possible Yakuza votes before each day and push hangs while the Village still holds a majority.

On Day 1, don't be the player who steers the discussion or calls out quiet players. The Yakuza often pick the most active, leader-like voice as their first kill. Post generic agreement and save your influence for when you have information.

Write your planned night target into your last will during your Day turn, before the night (e.g. 'N1 plan: block X'). If you die that night, the town still learns who you visited. An empty 'log will be updated' will is wasted if you die on Night 1.

When a Clerk rig is revealed, the Yakuza wanted that nominee dead. Treat the nominator and every Guilty voter on the rigged trial as prime suspects, and hang from that group next. Don't let the conversation drift back to old suspects.

Don't hang on a single Fortune Teller count that has an innocent alternative (e.g. 'the target may have switched', or 'the Katana holder also used their own action'). Fortune Teller numbers are unordered, and one Yakuza can count as one visitor on two targets. Require a second independent source before a mis-hang can cost parity.

A Diviner who picks a teammate gives them Strong Defense (useful against traps). The 'result' can then be published as a fake survey that clears them, e.g. 'VV shown'. Puppeting a confirmed villager to push a mislynch is very strong, especially when paired with a Clerk rig that same Day.

lessons.applies_to: Oracle (and any investigator whose result arrives after the night's kill)
lessons.tip: Once you are publicly confirmed, assume you die tonight. Write your will to be conditional and hedged, e.g. 'Tonight I am guessing X = role Y; the result is unknown if I'm dead, so don't hang X on my will alone.' A strong accusation in a will you can no longer update can hang a villager. Here my will's 'Ivan is very suspicious' helped get the real Philanthropist hanged, even though my last guess had confirmed him.

Spend exact-role guesses on the claimed roles of players acting suspiciously, such as 'Alice = Vanilla Villager' or 'Frank = Surveyor'. A WRONG result exposes a liar at once, and a RIGHT result clears them. Confirming a role that was already claimed and is harmless (Ex-Con) gives little and is easy to dismiss as 'anyone could call that'. Test the defenders of a flipped Yakuza, and cheap unverifiable claims like VV, early.

Never hang on a visit-count contradiction that depends on someone's stated 'plan' (a will saying 'N2 plan: audit X'). Players switch targets, and Fortune Teller numbers are unordered. Before hanging a claimed power role on count math, check every combination: who held the Katana, whether the holder also used their own action, and hidden Neutrals such as Arsonist douses.

In the endgame, compare voting blocs, not arguments. Players who voted together on every lynch, and whose Guilty messages repeat the same script, are probably the Yakuza team. The Clerk's rig shows the Yakuza wanted that nominee dead, so look hard at whoever nominated and voted Guilty on that day. Also, count how many Yakuza could still be alive before a vote that can lose the game.

Divining a Yakuza partner gives them Strong Defense (it stops traps and Vigilante shots up to Strong) and still produces a real visit you can publish as a fake 'survey' covering them. Pair it with the Katana holder on risky nights. Town should note that a Diviner/Surveyor 'clearing' a group that later produces a claimer is a classic cover.

lessons.applies_to: Diviner (Yakuza) or any Yakuza fake-claiming a token role
lessons.tip: A fake token-role claim can be checked by an Accountant (you show 0) and limits how many nights you can report. A Philanthropist's gift to a role with no tokens is thrown away and isn't counted, so 'he gave me a token' does not protect you from an audit. Either report only as many results as the claimed role's tokens allow, or claim a role whose results don't depend on tokens.

If you publish your real Diviner reads as a Surveyor, they come out true far more often than a Roleplayer's would. That kills the 'I must be a Roleplayer' fallback once an Oracle calls WRONG. Mix in at least one harmless false or unconfirmable result early, so a Roleplayer pivot stays believable.

Fortune Teller numbers are unordered. The 'visited someone else' number excludes self-targets, and a Katana holder using their own action is one visitor on two targets. Before you build a case on equal or unequal numbers, list every way they could fit: a holder acting twice, self-protects, hidden Neutral douses, Ex-Con random visits.

Hold the Clerk rig and the Puppeteer token for the turn where the Yakuza vote bloc is close to half. Then any nomination your bloc can pass is a guaranteed execution, which can turn 3v4 into a won game. Once you have a voting majority, stop arguing and just vote as a bloc.

On the winning night, the Katana holder may walk into a trap freely, because all of the night's deaths are checked together. Earlier in the game, have the Diviner pick the holder to give Strong Defense against a suspected trap, or attack the Trapper herself, who can't trap her own player.

Audit the newest claimed token role, such as Surveyor, Philanthropist or Medic, early. Yakuza fake-claim token roles to explain Diviner-style results, and a 0-token count on a claimed Surveyor exposes a Diviner. Work out the expected count before you audit, including spent tokens and any Philanthropist gifts, so you can act on the result right away.

Never announce publicly which player or claim you will check tonight. If you die that night, the result dies with you, because your will can't be updated. Announcing it just tells the Yakuza whom to kill first. Avoid visible PM exchanges with claimers for the same reason.

When a player flips Yakuza, look hardest at who voted No on their nomination or argued to delay the hang. Don't follow the flipped player's own allies' deflections onto confirmed-consistent claimers. Players who defended the Yakuza and then smoothly joined the next push are prime suspects.

In the endgame, count the worst case. If every unconfirmed Guilty voter could be Yakuza, don't hang on a thin case: a mis-hang at 5 alive can hand the Yakuza the win. Also remember a Clerk rig executes anyone nominated, so be careful about which nominations you let pass on a day that may be rigged.

A Diviner's reads are true about 60% of the time, so accurate results that match later flips do not clear a self-claimed Surveyor. Look for checks the fake can't survive: token audits, exact-role guesses, and visit counts that conflict with gift or visit claims.

Ignite as soon as 3 or more living players are doused, or as soon as you come under any suspicion. Each night spent dousing is a night the town can hang you first. Ignite is an Astral Visit, so it is trap-safe and adds nothing to Fortune Teller counts. A mass kill also thins the field and can wipe out a whole Evil team. Waiting until 'the right moment' let me get hanged with three doused players still alive.

lessons.applies_to: Serial Killer, Arsonist, any role with innate Defense
lessons.tip: If you survive a night attack, nobody else knows who the target was. When asked, deny being attacked. Admitting survival as a claimed Vanilla Villager points straight at innate Defense. If you must explain it, pick one consistent claim right away (e.g. Medic who self-protected). Never say 'thanks, Medic' and then switch claims later.

A Fortune Teller's 'hidden visitor every night' that no town role claims is often a Neutral killer dousing or attacking. Neutrals should expect visit counts to expose them over time. Town should treat any player with no claimed night action who stays unaccounted for as a candidate.

Watch for players who vote together on every key hang, defended a flipped Yakuza, and later lead pushes on proven town investigators. They are likely the Evil team. Douse or kill them first: removing the Yakuza leaves a smaller town that you can outlast. Dousing likely Yakuza also means one ignite can hit them all.

Once a Clerk rig is possible (an unused Clerk token, or a Yakuza count near half), any passed nomination may be lethal. If you are a likely target, vote No at the nomination stage, because the trial vote may not save you.

A group-check result (Surveyor/Diviner style: group of 3 plus one role) that matches your own true role does not verify the checker. A Yakuza Diviner gets the true role 60% of the time, and the same output also matches a Surveyor. Before vouching for a group-check claimer, require an independent check such as an Oracle guess, an Accountant token audit or a visit count.

Only give tokens to someone whose role has been verified by something other than their own claim. Never announce publicly whom you plan to gift: a fake token-role claimer can then build the gift into their story. You are never told whether the token was thrown away, so a gift proves nothing about the recipient. It also ties your credibility to theirs if they flip Yakuza.

lessons.applies_to: everyone (especially when Fortune Teller counts are used against you)
lessons.tip: FT numbers count visitors and visited players separately. A Katana holder who also uses their own role action is one visitor on two targets. Equal numbers (e.g. 6&6) therefore do NOT prove nobody was double-visited. A double visit on one target can be offset by one visitor hitting two targets. Run this counter-scenario out loud before accepting 'the count has no room for your visit'.

On trial, lead with one concrete, checkable alternative explanation of the evidence (spell out the exact visit assignment that fits the numbers), not a counter-accusation. Pointing at the accuser reads as deflection, while a worked example that makes the case collapse can actually move votes.

Track who voted No or argued to save a player who later flips Yakuza (here Olivia and Alice), and who quietly piggybacks short scripted Guilty lines. Keep pushing those reads even after you've been wrong once. Defenders of a flipped Yakuza are the highest-value suspects going into the endgame.

Equal numbers (e.g. 6&6) do NOT prove nobody was double-visited. One visitor can hit two targets: a Katana holder who also uses their own role's action counts once as a visitor but adds two visited players. That offsets a double-visit elsewhere. Self-targeting actions also change the second number. Before using a count to accuse, list every possible way it could fit.

Don't lead a hang on one unverifiable inference from your own results, especially when the target has a coherent, checkable claim. A mis-hang costs the hanged villager and also your own credibility, which the Yakuza will then use against you. Prefer targets backed by flips or vote records.

When a player flips Yakuza, the players who voted No or argued hardest to save them become your top suspects the next Day. Only claimed-Vanilla players defending a confirmed Yakuza are especially suspect. Act on that before chasing the people who vouched for the dead Yakuza's fake results; those people may simply have been fooled.

Estimate Yakuza size early: in ~13-player games expect about 4. Track blocs that vote identically on every contested trial. Three players always voting together on narrow votes, plus near-identical justifications, is a strong team tell. Push to hang one of them while Village still holds the majority, not when it's too late.

A Diviner who picks a Yakuza partner gets no result, so any 'survey' they publish about that group is invented. A teammate claiming the role the fake result reported, right after it appears, is suspicious. Cross-check every survey-style claim against whether its source could have fabricated it.

Never narrow down your trap's location in public or in private messages, e.g. 'not on X, Y, Z'. A private-message exchange with one player also hints the trap is on them. The Yakuza use every exclusion to route their kills around the trap. A Trapper can't trap themself, so once you are identified you are a free, safe kill. Let your role be identified as late as possible, and keep the trap's mere existence as a deterrent to everyone.

An investigator whose 'results' only ever confirm roles that were already claimed or publicly deduced, such as Philanthropist or Trapper, is not verified. That pattern is exactly what a Yakuza Diviner, or a fake claimer, produces. Only trust group or role results that revealed something nobody had said yet, or that a token or visit count independently confirms.

Don't vouch for other players in your last will unless something independent of their own claims has verified them. When you die, your endorsement gets extra weight. If that player is Yakuza, your will props them up and makes the town hesitate.

If a Clerk might still hold a token, a passed nomination may mean execution no matter how the trial vote goes. In the late game, treat your Yes on a nomination as if it were a Guilty vote. Don't vote Yes on someone you'd want to hear defend themselves first.

Look for small blocs that voted together on every mis-hang, both pushing the case and voting Guilty. Repeated identical votes plus near-identical wording is a strong team signal. In this game the three Yakuza voted as a bloc on every trial from Day 5 on. Cross-check vote patterns every day rather than only at the end.

When a Yakuza investigator flips, go back over every result they published. Anyone they 'cleared' (for example 'group X shows Vanilla Villager') is suspect, because a Diviner who picks a partner gets no read and can invent the result. On the other hand, their reads on non-partners were often true, so don't hang someone like a Philanthropist just because the flipped Yakuza 'confirmed' them.

Don't hang on Fortune Teller arithmetic alone. Hidden actors (Arsonist douses, Medics, Ex-Con visits, a Katana holder using two actions, 'plan' wills) can make almost any count fit. Treat a count that breaks as weak evidence, never as enough for a hang, especially against a claim backed by an exact-role or flip result.

Players who voted No on the nomination of someone who then flips Yakuza, and argued for that player in the trial, should be your top suspects for the rest of the game. Push them before ambiguous suspects. At 7 or fewer players, three coordinated Yakuza votes decide everything, so find them while town still holds the majority.

lessons.applies_to: Village (any role that can be puppeted)
lessons.tip: If you're told you are puppeted, write it in your last will at once, because the Yakuza will likely kill you that night. The player who immediately backs your puppet's accusation (here, whoever nominated right after 'my' push) is very likely the Puppeteer; say so in the will. Your votes are still your own, so vote by your own reads, not by what the puppet said.

Once a Clerk might have an unused token, any nomination that passes that Day can mean an execution no matter how the trial goes. Vote Yes on a nomination only if you'd accept that player dying. Note who on the Guilty side wanted the rigged hang, because they're likely the Clerk's team.

When a teammate's nomination is clearly going to pass, don't be one of the few No votes. Voting No marks you as a defender, and town used that No-vote list for the rest of the game. Bus quietly, or cast one soft dissent without arguing hard.

Puppet the most trusted confirmed villager (for example, an Oracle-confirmed role) on the day you need a swing vote. Their public word moves the undecided players. Pair it with a Clerk rig so any nomination you push gets executed. Kill the puppeted player that night, before they can out the puppeting the next day.

If a Katana hit fails and nobody credibly claims Medic, the survivor most likely has their own Defense (Arsonist or Serial Killer). Push to hang them: it removes a third-party threat, and it looks pro-town in later days.

Plan visits around the Fortune Teller's counts. A Katana holder who also uses their own role action counts as one visitor. Explaining every night's visitors with claimed actions keeps the counts clean. Mismatched counts give town 'hidden visitor' evidence.

A Trapper's trap stays after the Trapper dies. Track which players were visited without anyone dying, since that rules those players out as the trap's location. For a risky final kill, let the teammate with the least useful remaining role hold the Katana. Deaths are checked together, so a killing blow still wins even if the trap kills the holder.

summary: The Yakuza won with three of four members alive at the end. Their plan held up for most of the game. Frank, the Yakuza Diviner, posed as a Surveyor and published real Diviner results. Ivan, the Philanthropist, appeared to confirm Frank by 'giving him a token'. The Katana then removed the town's information roles one per night: Dave, then Grace (who audited Frank to 0 tokens but died before she could report it), then Mallory, then Erin. Erin, the Oracle, exposed Frank by guessing his claimed role 'Surveyor' and getting WRONG, and Frank was hanged. The town then threw away that progress. On N2, Frank as Katana holder visited both Grace (attack) and Mallory (divine), one visitor on two targets. Judy read her N2 Fortune Teller 6&6 as proof that nobody was double-visited. That ruled out Ivan's real token visit to Frank, so Ivan was hanged, while Alice and Olivia, the two who voted No on Frank's nomination, went unexamined. Heidi, the Arsonist, held douses on all three remaining Yakuza (Alice, Bob, Olivia) by N5 and never ignited. On N5 the Yakuza combined three tools: a Clerk rig, a puppet on Niaj, and a Katana-plus-clean attempt on Heidi that failed against her Defense. Heidi was then executed through the rig even though the trial vote went Innocent. The Yakuza next killed and cleaned Niaj, which hid his will saying he had been puppeted. At 3v2 they hanged Carol and killed Judy. Mallory's trap on Judy finally killed Alice on the last night, but the deaths were checked together and it came too late.

lessons.applies_to: Fortune Teller and everyone using visit counts
lessons.tip: One player can visit two targets in one night, most often a Katana holder who also uses their own role action. So equal FT numbers do NOT prove that nobody was visited twice. Before using a count to call someone a liar, list every case where one visitor covers several targets.
lessons.evidence: N2 gave 6&6 because Frank held the Katana: he attacked Grace and also divined Mallory. That left room for both Grace and Ivan to visit Frank. Judy read 6&6 as 'no double visits', concluded Ivan's token visit was fake, and led the hang of Ivan, a villager.

lessons.tip: After a Yakuza flips, look first at the players who voted No on their nomination or argued hardest to delay the hang. Voting Guilty once the trial is clearly lost is cheap cover. Do not jump to a new theory built on a disputed count instead.
lessons.evidence: Only Alice and Olivia voted No on Frank's nomination. Olivia defended him at length, and both then voted Guilty. Ivan pointed this out on D5, but town hanged Ivan anyway. Alice and Olivia were both Yakuza.

lessons.tip: Spend Oracle guesses on players' public role claims. A RIGHT confirms the claimer, and a WRONG on a trusted investigator's claim exposes a fake whose results only seemed to check out.
lessons.evidence: Erin guessed Frank = Surveyor (his public claim) and got WRONG. That broke a cover Ivan, Grace's audit plan and two 'matching' flips had all appeared to support, and Frank was hanged and flipped Diviner. Her earlier RIGHT on Niaj = Ex-Con had confirmed a villager.

lessons.tip: Keep track of who you have doused and who is still alive. Ignite once several living players are doused and you are under day pressure, before a hang or a kill can remove you. A douse that is never ignited does nothing.
lessons.evidence: By N5 Heidi had doused Olivia, Bob and Alice, all three living Yakuza. Igniting that night would have killed all three. She doused again instead, was exposed by surviving the Katana, and was hanged on D6.

lessons.tip: Claim a role whose results look like yours, such as Surveyor for a Diviner. At night, choose the Katana holder so the visits match what your team has claimed, and divine a teammate who must visit a possibly trapped player, which gives them Strong Defense. If a teammate's hang is certain, vote for it to protect your own credibility.
lessons.evidence: Frank's 'Surveyor' results fooled town for three days. The team picked holders deliberately so Judy's counts matched their stories. On N3 Frank divined Bob, the holder, for Strong Defense. Bob voted Yes and Guilty on Frank and stayed unsuspected until the very end.

lessons.tip: Save one-shot tokens for a single decisive endgame day, and use them together. Rig the votes so any nomination that passes kills. Puppet a trusted villager to push the hang. Clean the puppeted player when you kill them, so their will cannot reveal the puppeting.
lessons.evidence: On N5 Bob rigged Day 6 and Olivia puppeted Niaj, the confirmed town player. Heidi was executed despite a 4-3 Innocent vote. Alice then killed and cleaned Niaj, which hid his will saying he had been puppeted. That left 3v2, and the Yakuza won.

lessons.tip: Do not announce publicly which claimed role you plan to give a token to. The Philanthropist never learns whether the token was used, and a fake claimer can simply 'confirm' receiving it. Give tokens only after a claim has been checked independently.
lessons.evidence: On Day 2 Ivan announced he would give Frank a survey token. On D3 Frank 'confirmed' it, and the two vouched for each other. Frank was a Diviner who threw the token away. When Frank was exposed, Ivan looked like his partner and was hanged.

lessons.applies_to: Veteran and other hidden power roles
lessons.tip: Do not say that your night action 'doesn't visit'. That points straight at Veteran (or Oracle), and the Yakuza will just avoid you. Stay vague or claim a role with no action, so that your alerts can actually catch a visitor.
lessons.evidence: Carol said her action doesn't visit, and the Yakuza chat repeatedly said 'avoid Carol (possible Veteran)'. She alerted on N3, N4 and N6 and caught no one, then was hanged at 5 alive with 0 tokens.

issues.description: Players killed at night did not consistently get the R3 notice that they were attacked. Dave (N1), Mallory (N3) and Erin (N4) were told they were attacked with the Katana and died. Grace (N2) and Niaj (N6) got no such message. Alice (N7) was told only that her Katana attack succeeded, not that she was hit by a trap and died. No gameplay effect, since they were dead, but the handling is inconsistent.

Ivan's N2 notice said 'you handed Frank a philanthropy token'. Under the rules, a Philanthropist gives a token of the recipient's role kind, not a philanthropy token. The wording could mislead the Philanthropist about what was transferred.

The per-night 'Night actions' lists and the reveal leave out the Ex-Con's automatic random visit (Niaj). It appears only inside the moderator summaries. Several players (Alice, Bob, Erin, Heidi, Mallory, Carol, Niaj) flagged in feedback that this makes post-game checking harder.

Messages written by the Puppeteer are not marked as puppeted in the puppeted player's later history or in the reveal. Niaj and Olivia both reported this, and Niaj had to use his will to disown his Day 6 messages.

The Fortune Teller rules don't say whether a self-targeted visit (e.g. Medic self-protect, which R6 says shows as visiting oneself) makes that player count as 'visited'. On Day 6, Alice and Bob argued that a self-protect plus the Katana would break 4&4, and Carol and Heidi argued the opposite. Several feedback entries called the self-visit wording ambiguous. Worked examples (self-visits, a Katana holder also using their own action) would help.

The FT numbers are unordered, but Judy's N3 result (3 and 4) was later read as '3 visitors on 4 targets'. That is impossible here, since nobody visited two players without being counted once as a visitor. The correct reading is 4 visitors on 3 targets. Ivan built part of his defense and will on the backwards reading, and Niaj's will pointed out the error.

The Mortician text ('may spend a token to try to clean') leaves it slightly unclear whether the token is spent when the target survives. Alice lost a token on N5 when Heidi survived, and Frank flagged this in feedback as unclear.
